seo.title: Karmic tail 18 18 9 compatibility: The Moon, The Moon, The Hermit
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 18 9 compatibility: two Moons and The Hermit as the main task, read through the legend of Melusine, who had a tail on Saturdays.

title: Karmic tail 18-18-9 in compatibility: Melusine's Saturday
short: The 18-18-9 tail turns up in one couple in 452: The Moon, The Moon again, and The Hermit. Two nights in a row and a lantern at the end. The couple enters the task through a secret: the two understand each other without words and protect what goes unasked (The Moon). They live through the middle on guesswork: behind the other's closed door each sees something of their own (The Moon again). The main task is The Hermit: each has a room of their own, but solitude does not harden into a wall, and silence does not pile up grievances.

sections.h2: What the 18-18-9 tail means in compatibility
paragraphs: The three numbers of a couple's tail come from two personal matrices: each point is the sum of the matching points of the two partners, reduced to 22. They are read from the entry to the main task, and the last of the three matters most.

ul: **Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** What the couple wants together and the language it agrees in. Here that is a secret for two: private words, understanding from half a phrase, care for whatever the other keeps quiet about. The point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish also works as resistance: a straight question feels like a breach of the agreement.
**Middle of the task — 18, The Moon again.** How the couple travels from the wish to the task. By guesswork: whatever went unasked, each fills in alone, and imagination does the work of two.

**Main task — 9, The Hermit.** What the couple has to learn. In a couple The Hermit means time and a place of one's own for each, love shown in deeds, talk that goes to the point. In the minus, each is on their own: hard things pile up in silence, and at a difficult moment both retreat into their shells.

paragraphs: In short, an 18-18-9 couple comes together over a secret, lives on guesses and learns a solitude that does not become a wall. This is not a forecast and not a verdict. The tail shows what such a couple stumbles over and what its own life teaches it, not what will happen to it. To see how this looks from the inside, a story is needed, and the best one turned up in the fourteenth century.

sections.h2: The Moon at the entry: a marriage made at a fountain
paragraphs: Young Raymondin, nephew of the Count of Poitiers, is hunting boar with his uncle, and night finds the two of them alone in the forest. The count decides to wait "until the moon has risen" (here and below the romance is quoted in our own translation from the Middle French), and Raymondin lights a fire. The moon rises, the romance takes note of it — bright, "without spot or shadow" — and the count, a reader of the stars, weeps: he has read in the sky that whoever kills his lord at this hour will become the greatest of his line. Then a boar comes out of the thicket, Raymondin's blow glances off, and the count is dead.

Raymondin rides wherever the horse takes him, half asleep in the saddle with grief. "And the moon shone bright," the author writes once more. Around midnight the horse brings him to the Fountain of Thirst, a place where, people said, wonders happened. Three ladies are at the water. The first of them takes the horse by the bridle, wakes the rider and calls him by his name. "There is no use hiding it from me: I know well how thou didst slay thy lord by mischance," she says. She also knows what the count read in the stars.

She offers to become his wife and promises to make him the greatest of his line. There is one condition, and the oath runs both ways. He swears that on Saturdays he will never try to see her or find out where she is. She swears on the peril of her soul that on that day she will do nothing that does not serve his honour, and **will think only of how to raise him and his house**. Then she teaches him the first secret of their marriage: go back to the town, act astonished and wait for the body to be brought in — everyone will take the wound for the mark of a boar's tusks.

This is what the union rests on in its first night. He is hiding something terrible, his uncle's death. She already knows it, asks for no confession and suggests herself how to cover it up. She is hiding her own thing, the Saturday. He promises not to ask. The two secrets together become the agreement: I will keep yours, you leave mine alone.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements and a common language. In the couple reading this point carries a second label as well — "Common language". Here The Moon gives a start many will recognise. Two people understand each other from half a phrase and read each other's mood from footsteps in the hall. They have jokes no outsider would get. Nobody has to explain why the other has been quiet all evening. On the very first night Melusine knows more about Raymondin than he would have dared to tell, and she asks him nothing. Anyone who began like this remembers the feeling: you are seen right through and not judged.

But the point stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. A "don't ask" agreement works until a question comes up. Then the couple has no words for it: to ask means breaking the very thing it all began with. This beginning has a second shadow too. Raymondin also agrees because he has nowhere to go: the romance says outright that he feels like an exile. Among the difficulties of The Moon in a couple Lisovskaya names a union in which people hide from other troubles, and an image created at the start that later collapses. Melusine came into his life as a rescuer with a ready plan. It is exactly this image that will collapse.

sections.h2: The second Moon: a hole in the door and wax from an old letter
paragraphs: After that the romance spends a long time on prosperity. Melusine builds fortresses and towns, bears ten sons and vanishes on Saturdays, and Raymondin keeps his word. From outside no secret can be seen — only a lady of the house who is busy one day a week.

A guest brings the secret in. On a Saturday before dinner Raymondin's brother, the Count of Forez, arrives, asks where his sister-in-law is and says what he came to say: "All over the country the talk is that on Saturdays your wife is with another man. Others insist she is a fairy who does penance on Saturdays. I don't know which to believe."

Both of the brother's versions fit into one line of Waite's divinatory meanings for The Moon: "Hidden enemies, danger, calumny, darkness, terror, deception, occult forces, error." Calumny and occult forces sit in one list, just as they sit in one sentence of the Count of Forez. One version is false, the other true, and by moonlight they have the same outline.

Raymondin pushes the table away, takes his sword and goes where in all those years he had never gone. There is an iron door. He turns the point until he has made a hole, and looks. Melusine is sitting in a marble bath. Down to the waist she is a woman combing her hair, and below that is a serpent's tail "as thick as a herring barrel", and she beats the water with it so hard that the spray reaches the vault.

There is no lover. There is what she carries alone: a curse and a penance he knew nothing about. "Ah, my love," he says at the door, "now I have betrayed you through my brother's wicked urging and broken my oath." Then he does the thing that makes the whole romance worth reading: **he takes the wax from an old letter and seals up the hole**.

This is the second Moon. In the morning Melusine lies down beside him; he pretends to be asleep, sighs, and when she asks, says he has had a touch of fever. She knows he has seen. He thinks she does not know. She stays silent because he has told no one. Now the couple has two secrets: the old one, what is behind the door, and a new, shared one, that the door was opened. Both are sealed with wax.

Waite's divinatory list for The Hermit reads like an inventory of that night: "Prudence, circumspection; also and especially treason, dissimulation", and reversed, "Concealment, disguise" and "fear". "I have betrayed you", the wax on the door, the feigned sleep, her calm face as if nothing had happened. The main task is still far off, and The Hermit is already standing behind the door.

The second night belongs to the couple alone. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is made from the entry and the main task, and with the same ends it would hold a nine: 18 + 9 = 27 → 9. A single person has no way of getting a Moon in the middle. In a couple the middle is made from the partners' middles — 3 + 15 or 9 + 9 — and the result is 18. **No one can make the second Moon alone; it takes two**, and it is built from what each lived through before they met.

In everyday life it looks ordinary. A glance at someone else's phone screen, a letter read by the wrong person, a conversation overheard from the corridor. Or someone's passing remark: "What's all this about Thursdays?" What follows is not a row but wax: he saw and said nothing, she guessed and gave no sign. Among the minuses of The Moon in a couple Lisovskaya names jealousy and grievances built on invented stories, and the state in which it is unclear whether the two are friends or enemies. The treacherous part is that the story may not be invented at all: Raymondin saw the truth. But a truth that cannot be spoken works like a fiction. It lives in the imagination and grows there.

In Wen's reading of The Moon reversed there is a sentence that might have been written about the wax: "The repressed latent will always surface, and any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing." In the romance that is how it goes, only not at once.

sections.h2: The Hermit: seven cells on a cliff
paragraphs: Years later grief strikes the family: one of the sons, Geoffroy Big Tooth, burns down in a rage the abbey where his brother was a monk. Raymondin sits in his room, broken, and does not return his wife's greeting. Melusine comes to comfort him, speaks calmly and sensibly, and suggests rebuilding the abbey. He understands that she is right — the romance says so plainly — but his anger is stronger. And in front of the barons, before the whole court, he cries: "Ah, false serpent! By God, thou and thy deeds are nothing but a phantom."

The word "phantom" (fantosme) has already sounded in the romance — on the first night, at the fountain. Back then Melusine said it herself: I know thou thinkest this a phantom or the devil's work, but I am from God. The fear Raymondin did not say aloud by the water, she named for him. Years later he said it himself, in front of everyone. **A marriage that began with an unspoken fear ended with that very word**.

Melusine faints, and when she comes to, she says the sentence that explains the whole tail: "Because thou hadst revealed it to no one, I had forgiven thee in my heart, though I never said a word to thee about it." The look through the hole had been forgiven. What proved unforgivable was something else — a secret carried out to other people. As long as what he had seen stayed between the two of them, it was their shared Moon. Shouted in front of witnesses, it became a weapon. Lisovskaya lists exactly this among the difficulties of The Moon in a couple: the partner's secrets become weapons.

From here The Hermit arrives in its minus, as two solitudes. Melusine says goodbye: as long as he lives she will always take comfort in looking at him, but he will never see her in a woman's shape again. She leaps onto the window ledge, turns into a serpent, circles the fortress three times crying out and flies away; the print of her foot, the author assures us, can still be seen on the window stone. The duke the romance was written for later commissioned the Limbourg brothers to paint the Très Riches Heures, and in its miniature for March a gilded winged serpent flies over the castle of Lusignan.

Every evening she comes to the two youngest children, warms them by the fire and comforts them as best she can. The nurses see her but dare not say a word. Raymondin learns of it from the nurses and hopes to win her back — in vain. "And from then on no one ever saw him laugh."

The last chapter of his life is Montserrat, the mountain near Barcelona. There, on a sheer cliff, are seven cells, one above the other, with an order of their own: the lowest hermit hauls up the food for all seven, takes his share and passes the rest higher. Raymondin becomes one of the seven. He tells nothing about himself: noble visitors come, the King of Aragon himself asks who he is and where he comes from — and never finds out. The man who gave away another's secret ends his life as the keeper of his own.

Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through its minus, and the minus of The Hermit in a couple sounds like the end of the romance: each on their own, hard things piling up in silence, a retreat into the shell instead of help at a difficult moment. The tasks she sets are these: in hard times do not hide but help; share and listen; sense when to support and when to leave alone; know the limits of what is allowed. The legend shows each of them from the wrong side. Raymondin crossed the limit when he made the hole, and hid when grief came. Melusine never once said what she bore her Saturday for, not even in farewell: of this, she says, "I cannot and will not speak further." Both of them are hermits here.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: two personal nines make one Moon
paragraphs: Now to what is written in the numbers and is the same for every couple with this tail. Running through all the dates shows that 18-18-9 comes from exactly two combinations of personal tails. They are 9-15-6 + 9-3-21 (82% of such couples) and 9-9-18 + 9-9-18 (18%). There is no third combination.

The key clue is the first numbers. **Both partners' personal tails begin with a nine** — always, in every such couple. Nine is The Hermit, and two nines add up to 18, The Moon. The couple's entry to the task is literally made of two hermits: two people who each need a closed room of their own get a shared secret together. As in the romance: he came to the fountain with his secret, she with her Saturday.

The couple reading shows this in one more place. Lisovskaya calls the first point of the personal tail the semi-dual and links it to wishes. The site shows it in the sphere "Compatibility of characters" when one partner's energy appears in the other's chart. For 18-18-9 couples The Hermit is always there on the "Wishes" line: both want solitude, and each recognises that wish in the other.

The couple's middle: 3 + 15, The Empress and The Devil, or 9 + 9, two Hermits again. The main task: 6 + 21 = 27 → 9, The Lovers and The World, or 18 + 18 = 36 → 9, two Moons. In the first combination the partners' main tasks are a choice and a whole world, and together they give the couple The Hermit's lantern. In the second each has a Moon of their own, and two personal nights add up to one shared task — to light a lamp. The same arithmetic works inside the tail itself: The Moon plus The Moon, 18 + 18, reduces to its last card.

The centre of the couple's chart, its atmosphere, is The Hermit for 82% of such couples and The Moon for 18%. In "The couple's values" The Hermit appears in 57.7% and The Moon in 42.3%. In 41.9% of couples The Hermit stands at once in the main task, the centre and the values. No other cards occur in these five places — entry, middle, main task, centre and values — only The Moon and The Hermit. It is as if the couple lived in two rooms, a night room and a room with a lamp, and walked between them.
One last thing: the tail is rare. It occurs in one couple in 452 (0.221%) and ranks 71st of the 97 couple tails.
The legend cannot be rewritten, but a couple's own story can. The hints lie in the text of the romance itself.

**Say the Saturday out loud.** The better half of the agreement was hers: on that day I will think only of how to raise you. A solitude that has been declared not to be against the partner stops being a door behind which anything can be imagined. Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Moon to accept the other's need to withdraw: it is a way of getting one's strength back, not a lack of love. It is easier to accept once it has a name: "I need an evening on my own", and why, and that it is not about the other.

**Ask with words, not with a sword.** The "don't ask" agreement is what made the sword inevitable: Raymondin had no way to ask except a hole in the door. An 18-18-9 couple would do well to rewrite that clause: asking is allowed, and the answer can be as much as one is able to give. "I'm not ready to tell yet, but it's not about another person" is an answer too, and a better one than wax.

**What has been seen stays between the two.** Melusine forgave the look because it stayed between them. If one partner learns something the other was not showing, that knowledge is the couple's shared secret, not a trump card in a quarrel and not a topic for the relatives.

**Check rumours with the partner, not at the door.** The brother brought two rumours and did not know himself which to believe. For The Moon in a couple Lisovskaya gives simple rules: do not invent things on the other's behalf, and do not unload your fears onto them.

**In grief, do not lock yourselves away from each other.** Raymondin did not answer the wife who came to comfort him. For The Hermit in a couple it helps to go into silence not away from the partner but together, when things are bad for both.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: bread from cell to cell
paragraphs: In the plus these two cards give a couple something rare. The Moon brings a sensitivity that lets one hear the other's mood from the next room, games and fantasies for two, the feeling of being desired and, as Lisovskaya writes, a habit of discovering something new in the partner every year. The Hermit brings a corner and an hour of one's own for each, attention to small things, a late-night conversation after which the two can sit in silence for a long time. Melusine, incidentally, loved in exactly this way — in deeds: fortresses, towns, advice. The romance never tires of repeating that everyone spoke well of her.

The best image of the strong version comes at the end of the romance, on Montserrat. Seven cells on a cliff are seven closed doors, and nobody forces their way in on anybody. But the bread rises from below, hand to hand, and each solitude feeds the next. That is what an 18-18-9 couple looks like once it has solved its task. Each has a room and a Saturday of their own, the secret stays a garden and not a fog, and what passes through the wall is not suspicion but bread.
The first partner's personal tail is 9-3-21, the second's is 9-15-6. The couple's points are added pair by pair and reduced to 22.

The main trap in the calculation is the middle. If, out of habit from the personal matrix, one adds the ends, 18 + 9 = 27 → 9, the result is 18-9-9, which is a different couple tail. The couple's middle is made only from the partners' middles. "The couple's values" here are The Hermit too: they are recalculated from the couple's own sums. A plain sum of the personal values, 9 + 9, would give The Moon.

The same numbers in a different order set a different task. In 9-18-18 (1.228% of couples, The Moon in the centre for 66.8%) the couple enters through The Hermit, through caution and distance, and its main task is The Moon: learning to see each other without fog. In 18-9-18 (0.963%, The Moon in the centre for 91.1%) the entry is through a secret, the middle through solitude, and the main task is The Moon again. In 18-18-9 the fog comes first and builds up over two points in a row, and at the end stands The Hermit's task — a solitude that does not become a wall.

intro: This couple was described more than six hundred years ago. In August 1393 Jean d'Arras finished a romance for Jean, Duke of Berry, about the fairy Melusine, ancestress of the house of Lusignan. Her husband swore never to look for her on Saturdays. On Saturdays she had a tail.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-18-9 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a tail of the couple's matrix: The Moon at the entry to the task, The Moon in the middle and The Hermit as the main task. The couple comes together over a shared secret and wordless understanding, lives the path on guesswork and learns a solitude that does not turn into a wall: each has a room of their own, but hard things are said out loud.

faq.q: Is the 18-18-9 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not an outcome. The Moon and The Hermit give a couple rare sensitivity and respect for each other's space; the difficulty is that what goes unsaid easily turns into fog. The method gives no compatibility percentages and no verdicts.

faq.q: Can 18-18-9 occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is made from the entry and the main task, and with these ends it would hold a nine (18 + 9 → 9). The couple tail 18-18-9 is possible because its middle is the sum of the two partners' middles.

faq.q: How can a couple tell it has the 18-18-9 tail?
faq.a: By calculating compatibility from the two birth dates. In every such couple both personal tails begin with a nine: the partners have either 9-15-6 and 9-3-21, or 9-9-18 each.

report: Melusine's husband swore never to look for her on Saturdays. On Saturdays she had a tail. Jean d'Arras wrote the legend down in 1393, and the couple tail 18-18-9 runs through it almost in order: The Moon at the entry to the task, The Moon in the middle, The Hermit as the main task. The strangest thing in it is that the husband who spied on the secret was forgiven. Something else destroyed the marriage.

report.h3: A union sealed on two secrets

At the water a fairy calls him by his name: "There is no use hiding it from me: I know well how thou didst slay thy lord by mischance." She asks for no confession and suggests herself how to cover up the death. In return comes an oath: never to look for her on Saturdays and never to find out where she is. Melusine herself swears that on that day she will think only of how to raise him and his house.

For years Raymondin keeps his word. Then his brother arrives and repeats the gossip: on Saturdays the wife is with another man, or perhaps she is a fairy doing penance — "I don't know which to believe." Raymondin takes his sword, makes a hole in the iron door and sees Melusine in a marble bath: a woman down to the waist, below it a serpent's tail. There is no lover. There is what she carries alone.

Then he does the thing that makes the legend worth knowing: **he takes the wax from an old letter and seals up the hole**. In the morning he pretends to be asleep. She knows he has seen, and stays silent because he has told no one. Now the couple has two secrets: what is behind the door, and that the door was opened.

This is the second Moon, the middle of the task. A single person has no way of getting it: in a personal matrix with the same ends the middle would hold a nine. In a couple the middle is made from the partners' middles, and the result is 18. No one can make the second night alone; it takes two. In everyday life it looks ordinary: a glance at someone else's phone screen, a conversation overheard from the corridor, someone's remark, "What's all this about Thursdays?" What follows is not a row but wax: he saw and said nothing, she guessed and gave no sign. A truth that cannot be spoken works like a fiction: it lives in the imagination and grows there.

Years later grief strikes the family. Melusine comes to comfort her husband, and in front of the whole court he cries: "Ah, false serpent! By God, thou and thy deeds are nothing but a phantom." When she comes to, she says the sentence that explains the whole tail: "Because thou hadst revealed it to no one, I had forgiven thee in my heart, though I never said a word to thee about it."

**The look through the hole had been forgiven. What proved unforgivable was a secret carried out to other people.** As long as what he had seen stayed between the two of them, it was their shared Moon. Shouted in front of witnesses, it became a weapon.

From here The Hermit arrives in its minus, as two solitudes. She flies away, yet every evening comes to warm the youngest children by the fire. He goes to Montserrat and to the end of his life tells no one who he is, not even the King of Aragon. The couple's main task is The Hermit, and in the minus it looks exactly like this: each on their own, hard things piling up in silence, both retreating into their shells at a difficult moment. Both are hermits in the legend: Raymondin crossed the limit and then hid in his grief, and Melusine never said what she bore her Saturday for.

The hints for a way out lie in the same legend. The Saturday is said out loud: a solitude that has been declared not to be against the partner stops being a door behind which anything can be imagined. The other's need to withdraw is a way of getting strength back, not a lack of love. Questions are asked with words, not with a sword: asking is allowed, the answer can be as much as one is able to give, and "not ready to tell yet" is better than wax. What has been seen stays between the two and does not become a trump card in a quarrel. In grief the two do not lock themselves away from each other.

On Montserrat there are seven cells on a sheer cliff, one above the other. The lowest hermit hauls up the food for all seven and passes it higher. **Seven closed doors, and each solitude feeds the next.** That is the strong version of 18-18-9: each has a room and a Saturday of their own, the secret stays a garden and not a fog, and what passes through the wall is not suspicion but bread.
